claims.claim: The style is unstable, veering from functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms and from an Anglo-Saxon to a Latinate lexicon.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: veers from purely functional modern thriller prose

claims.claim: The default setting of the style is lucid and functional.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: The default setting of Martin’s style is lucid and functional

claims.claim: Martin consistently chooses Anglo-Saxon words over Latinate ones, giving the prose a cumulative woodiness, antiquity and pithiness.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness

claims.claim: 'Oft', 'elsewise', 'amongst', 'whilst', 'much and more' and dropped -ly adverbs become annoying pseudo-medieval mannerisms.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014

claims.claim: Distorted words ('Ser', girls who have 'flowered') start silly but by sheer repetition come to seem natural.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term

claims.claim: Compounds like sellsword, smallfolk, ironborn, greenseer and weirwood are a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of the style.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style

claims.claim: Confrontations are done through terse, charged dialogue that delivers real dramatic shock.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014

claims.claim: Repeated 'cool' and 'still' in the Water Gardens passage may be haste or deliberate torpor-evoking repetition.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: signs of haste, or careful repetitions

claims.claim: Names in three registers (near-familiar, alien, exotic) work on a purely verbal level to pull the reader into a parallel universe.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: the text works on a purely verbal level

claims.claim: The style is uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'Some notes on George RR Martin's prose style', 31 Mar 2014
claims.quote: uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative

claims.claim: The archaic feel comes from the systematic exclusion of almost all Latin-, Greek- and French-derived words.
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words

claims.claim: Martin uses almost exclusively English prefixes (un-, be-, a-) and native suffixes (-craft, -dom, -ling, -ward).
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013
claims.quote: Martin uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes

claims.claim: Anglo-Saxon compounding lets Martin coin scores of evocative neologisms (archmaester, bannermen, skinchanger, weirwood).
claims.source: Simon (Books & Boots), 'George RR Martin's prose style – Affixes, compound and combination words', 8 Mar 2013

claims.claim: The result is prose that feels archaic; the medieval sense comes from filtered vocabulary, not stock phrases.

verdicts.trueWording: veers from purely functional modern thriller prose
verdicts.note: Page opens: style 'is unstable... it veers from purely functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms, from a lexicon of short, Anglo-Saxon words to one suddenly stuffed with neoclassical and latinate vocabulary.' Quote verbatim; every limb (instability, thriller-to-medievalism veer, Anglo-Saxon-to-Latinate lexicon) on the page. Raw HTML fetched by browser-UA curl, 200; quote matched by script.

verdicts.trueWording: The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional
verdicts.note: Section 1 'Crisp' reads: 'The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional:' followed by the Jon Snow dawn passage. Verbatim (page uses a curly apostrophe).

verdicts.trueWording: a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness
verdicts.note: Conclusion: 'he consistently chooses words of Anglo-Saxon origin and generally avoids Latinate and neoclassical vocabulary, thus giving his prose a cumulative feeling of woodiness, antiquity, pithiness.' Both limbs (the choosing, the cumulative effect) verbatim.

Section 9 'Cod medievalism' lists 'would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms': removing the -ly suffix from adverbs, 'Oft' instead of 'often', 'Elsewise', the amongst/whilst line quoted, and 'cod medieval phrases such as much and more'. All six items and the 'annoying mannerisms' framing are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term
verdicts.note: Section 5 'Distorting English': 'Ser', 'which starts out sounding silly but, by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term. Similarly, girls who have had their first period have flowered'. Both examples and the silly-then-natural arc are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms (of the compounds)
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim but belongs to section 6 'New coinages', whose examples are sept/septon/septa, maester, wildlings, pyromancer, holdfast, warg, damphair. The five words the claim names are all on the page but in the SEPARATE section 7 'New word combinations', where the page says only 'Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms' and that they 'build up a linguistic base for the otherness of his fantasy world' - no creative/enjoyable praise. Confirmed positionally: the praise phrase is on text line 73 under heading '6 New coinages'; the compound list is on line 77 under '7 New word combinations'. (The sibling 2013 post does call the compounds 'scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms' - see index 507 - but that is a different page from the one cited here.)
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the praise 'a highly creative and enjoyable aspect of his style' is said of the new coinages (sept, maester, warg), not of the compounds sellsword/smallfolk/ironborn/greenseer/weirwood

verdicts.note: Section 4 'Dramatic dialogue': 'Confrontations between opposing characters are done though [sic] terse, charged dialogue. As a reader on numerous occasions you experience a real dramatic shock...' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported (the page's 'though' is its own typo for 'through' and lies outside the quoted span).

verdicts.trueWording: the word paintings of the Water Palace of Lord Martell of Dorne
verdicts.note: Substantive limb is verbatim: '(I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage - of cool and still - are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.)' Haste-vs-deliberate-torpor and the two repeated words are exactly right. Only the location label diverges: the page introduces the quoted FFC40 passage as the 'Water Palace', never 'Water Gardens'. Relabel the passage and the claim is fully sourced.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the Water Gardens passage' - the page calls it the 'Water Palace of Lord Martell of Dorne'

verdicts.trueWording: the text works on a purely verbal level to draw you into a parallel universe
verdicts.note: Section 8 'New names' groups names into 'a) Similar names' (of names 'nearly recognisable but bent or distorted... nearly in a familiar world - but not quite'), 'b) Alien names', 'c) Exotic names', then: 'In these and related ways the text works on a purely verbal level to draw you into a parallel universe, whisperingly close to our English history and culture, yet bracingly alien and explosive.' Three registers and the verbal-level pull both supported.

verdicts.trueWording: uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative
verdicts.note: Closing line: 'The thoughts above are intended to shed further light on the distinctive strengths and achievements of his uneven but often wonderfully powerful and evocative style.' Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French
verdicts.note: Abstract: '...but by a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French or other languages, or foreign loan words, or the neo-classical coinages'. The archaic-effect limb is carried later on the same page: 'they feel that much more ubiquitous because there are so few words sourced from Latin, Greek or French... The result is to make his prose feel archaic.'

verdicts.trueWording: Martin uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes
verdicts.note: Prefix section: quote verbatim, 'Common examples are un- and be- forms', plus 'he conspicuously deploys the archaic prefix a- to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse'. Suffix section: 'Martin overwhelmingly uses forms which convey a deep sense of their Anglo-Saxon provenance. Notably common in his lexicon are: -craft, -dom, -en, -ful, -hood, -less, -ling, -ly, -ness, -ship, -some, -ward(s)'. All four named prefixes/suffix examples in the claim appear.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin uses this facility to coin scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms
verdicts.note: Compound-words section: 'The following compound words are found in... A Feast For Crows... an overwhelming tendency to use Anglo-Saxon or archaic source words to form compound words', then the quote, then a list opening 'archmaester, bannermen (minor families loyal to a great lord)...' and containing 'skinchanger (who can change into an animal)' and 'weirwood (the holy trees)'. All four examples and the Anglo-Saxon-compounding limb present.

verdicts.trueWording: derives not from a handful of obvious stock phrases, but from a carefully filtered Anglo-Saxon vocabulary
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in 'Some examples'. The second limb is the page's own conclusion: 'the strong sense the reader gets from Martin's novels of a fully-imagined, alternative, medieval fantasy world derives not from a handful of obvious stock phrases, but from Martin's deep and systematic deployment of a carefully filtered and defined, rich, evocative and highly pleasurable, Anglo-Saxon vocabulary.' The page even names the stock phrases it rejects ('prithee', 'Zounds', 'my liege').

verdicts.trueWording: Martin leans on words that I presume he thinks sound archaic and exotic. In reality they just sound ridiculous.
verdicts.note: Under 'Terrible Turns of Phrase Which Are Repeated Over and Over': '...in order to embellish his tales with a sense of the grandiose, Martin leans on words that I presume he thinks sound archaic and exotic. In reality they just sound ridiculous.' Both limbs verbatim; byline confirmed on page as 'Posted on March 21, 2012 by Asher Gelzer-Govatos'.
